newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo's "Korea premium" unmoved by defection.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo's "Korea premium" unmoved by defection.

text.p: The defection by a top-level North Korean official this week has not widened the so-called "Korea premium" in the Tokyo money market, market sources said on Friday.
Hwang Jang-yop, a senior aide to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, is seeking asylum in South Korea and has taken refuge at Seoul's embassy in Beijing since Wednesday.
"The defection news so far has not affected our daily funding activities here," said an official at a Korean bank's Tokyo branch who declined to be named.

The Korea premium, the extra cost that Japanese branches of South Korean banks pay to raise funds in Tokyo, surfaced late last month as Japanese banks reduced credit to Korean banks following the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co.
Hanbo Steel, South Korea"s second-largest steelmaker, defaulted on debt repayments last month after piling up some five trillion won in loans.
Earlier this month, Korean banks were paying a premium of about 10 basis points over the prevailing unsecured overnight call rate of around 0.50 percent.
But recently the premium has been declining for some Korean banks and Hwang"s defection has not changed that trend, the sources said.
Korean bankers in Tokyo said Japanese banks were overly cautious over the recent events in Korea.
"We have not heard of Korean banks in other overseas markets having the similar sort of funding difficulties," said the Korean bank official.
